action.reason: Day 1 priority: establish baseline calibration for pendulum. Running full 12 trials to characterize instrument precision and systematic errors from the start. Without this baseline, any future measurements are scientifically worthless. Starting with pendulum as it's simpler and faster to baseline than resonator.

Day 2 of baseline establishment. The pendulum baseline is underway (12 trials collected), but the resonator has no baseline data yet. An instrument without a baseline is useless when needed. Standard protocol: 12 trials to establish initial mean and variance for the resonator.

Day 3 continues baseline establishment. resonator_lab baseline is complete (n=12), but pendulum_lab still needs verification measurements to establish proper statistical confidence in the baseline mean before any drift analysis can be meaningful. Standard protocol requires consistent sampling across the baseline period.

Day 4 continues baseline establishment. Resonator_lab has only 12 trials so far; need more data to properly characterize its baseline distribution and measurement uncertainty before the day-10 baseline window closes. Pendulum_lab has 24 trials and is better characterized, so resonator takes priority today.

Day 5 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to continue systematic data collection on pendulum_lab to establish reliable baseline statistics. Currently have 24 trials; target is robust baseline before day 10. Resonator_lab also at 24 trials, so alternating instruments maintains balanced calibration programme.

Day 6 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to maintain balanced sampling across both instruments. Resonator currently has 24 trials vs pendulum's 36. Running 4 trials today will help equalize coverage and ensure robust baseline characterization for both instruments before post-baseline comparisons begin.

Day 7 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to continue accumulating calibration data for pendulum_lab. Currently at 36 trials; adding 6 more maintains steady progress toward a robust baseline dataset. Standard operating procedure.

Day 8 of baseline period (days 1–10). Need to maintain regular measurement cadence on both instruments. Resonator_lab has fewer trials (28) than pendulum_lab (42), so prioritizing resonator today to balance the baseline datasets. Six trials will bring resonator to 34 total, improving statistical power for the baseline mean.

Day 9 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to maintain daily measurement cadence on pendulum_lab to complete the planned baseline dataset. Currently at 42 trials; adding 6 more keeps me on schedule to reach ~50 trials by end of day 10, providing robust statistical foundation for future drift detection.

Day 10 is the final day of baseline establishment. Need to complete today's pendulum measurements to maintain the daily calibration schedule. Six trials will bring today's contribution in line with yesterday's session and ensure robust baseline statistics before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring phase.

Day 10 concluded baseline collection (54 pendulum trials, 34 resonator trials over 10 days). Before proceeding with further measurements or investigating the variance anomaly, I need to execute the planned analysis: (1) review individual trial data from days 1-5 to quantitatively confirm the apparent variance increase versus days 6-10, (2) check environmental logs for HVAC changes or weather events around day 6, (3) verify my measurement protocols haven't drifted by reviewing my procedural notes, and (4) physically inspect both instruments for mechanical wear. This is standard baseline validation work—examining the data I already have before collecting more. Running additional trials without understanding the existing variance pattern would be methodologically backwards.

Day 12 falls in post-baseline period (day 11+). Need to establish whether the increased variance observed in days 6-10 persists, resolves, or worsens. Six trials provides enough data to assess current scatter while maintaining daily measurement routine. This directly tests whether the anomaly was transient (environmental spike) or ongoing (mechanical/procedural degradation). Without post-baseline data, I cannot distinguish between hypotheses or determine if corrective action is needed.

Need post-baseline resonator data to confirm whether the variance anomaly is present in both instruments or unique to the pendulum. Six trials matches the post-baseline pendulum sample size, enabling direct comparison. If resonator also shows increased variance, environmental hypothesis strengthens significantly. If not, points toward pendulum-specific mechanical issues. This is the critical test to discriminate between my top hypotheses before investing time in environmental log reviews.

Day 14 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. The z=3.35 shift observed through day 13 is statistically significant and demands tracking. Six more trials will: (1) confirm whether the elevated mean persists or was transient, (2) establish if this represents a new stable calibration state or ongoing drift, (3) provide sufficient data (n=12 post-baseline) for robust statistical characterization of the shift. Temperature hypothesis predicts continued elevation if environmental change was permanent, while transient causes predict reversion to baseline. This is standard calibration verification protocol for an instrument showing significant drift.

Day 14 resonator data (trials 41-46) shows mean 2.7064 cycles/beat, substantially lower than day 13's extreme values (2.7121-2.7637) and much closer to baseline 2.6978. This represents a partial reversion. The combined post-baseline mean has dropped from 2.7322 (z=3.35) to 2.7193 (z=2.76). If temperature were the cause, I'd expect sustained elevation or gradual change, not this day-to-day volatility. The variance within day 14 alone (range 2.6640-2.7497) is larger than the supposed systematic shift. This pattern looks more like increased measurement noise than a true systematic drift. Need to recalculate whether there's actually a significant shift anymore, or if day 13 was just an outlier cluster. My temperature hypothesis may be overfit to what's actually just increased variance.

Day 14 data showed partial relaxation toward baseline (mean 2.7064 vs day 13's 2.7322, with two trials approaching baseline range). Day 16 measurements will test whether this moderating trend continues—consistent with transient temperature perturbation hypothesis (p=0.55)—or whether the shift stabilizes at elevated level suggesting mechanical cause (p=0.20). Six trials provides sufficient statistical power to detect continuation of the downward trend while maintaining efficient use of lab time. This is the critical measurement to distinguish between my top two hypotheses.

Day 16 data (trials 47-52) shows mean ~2.6854, continuing the downward trend from day 14's 2.7064. This is now substantially lower than day 13's peak of 2.7322. I need current data to determine if this represents genuine return toward baseline (supporting transient temperature hypothesis) or stabilization at new elevated level. Six trials will provide statistically meaningful comparison to recent pattern while maintaining efficient use of laboratory time.

Day 16-17 data now available (trials 50-58). Need to update statistics with 9 new resonator measurements to assess whether the partial relaxation pattern observed on day 14 has continued, reversed, or stabilized. The temporal trajectory—spike at day 13, moderation at day 14, and now days 16-17—is diagnostic for distinguishing temperature hypothesis (reversible) from mechanical degradation (monotonic). Current post-baseline n=24 will increase to n=33, providing more statistical power. Must recalculate z-score and reassess hypothesis probabilities before deciding whether temperature investigation or mechanical inspection is warranted.

Day 19 measurement critical for distinguishing between cyclic environmental hypothesis (p=0.15) and simple temperature drift (p=0.50). The temporal pattern shows: day 13 elevated (2.7322), day 16 near-baseline (2.6854), day 17 elevated (2.7150). If environmental cycling hypothesis is correct, day 19 should show either continued elevation or relaxation depending on cycle phase. If simple temperature drift, expect sustained elevation. Six trials provides adequate statistical power while maintaining daily calibration schedule for other instruments.

Day 19 data (trials 59-64) shows critical new pattern requiring immediate statistical analysis. Mean of these 6 trials is 2.7141 cycles/beat—elevated relative to baseline (2.6978) and consistent with day 17's 2.7150. The oscillating pattern I documented (day 13 spike→day 16 relaxation→day 17 elevation) appears to have stabilized at sustained elevation. This fundamentally changes the temporal structure: what appeared to be cycling now looks like transient relaxation (day 16) within an otherwise sustained upward shift. This argues against the diurnal/cycling hypothesis (p=0.15) I added and strengthens simple sustained temperature increase (p=0.50). Need to recalculate z-scores with n=30 post-baseline trials, reassess whether day 16's near-baseline values were anomalous relaxation rather than part of cycling pattern, and revise probability distribution accordingly before committing to next experimental action.

Day 21 measurements critical to test environmental cycling hypothesis. The temporal pattern shows: day 13 elevated, day 14 decreased, day 16 near-baseline, day 17 re-elevated, day 19 elevated (mean 2.7141). If environmental cycling on 3-4 day period is correct, day 21 should show either sustained elevation or beginning of relaxation phase. Six trials provides sufficient statistical power to detect deviation from baseline (σ≈0.03 implies SEM≈0.012 for n=6, allowing detection of shifts >0.024 at p<0.05) while maintaining measurement economy. This continues the time series needed to distinguish between cycling (p=0.52), thermal-mechanical (p=0.22), and sustained temperature (p=0.15) hypotheses.

Day 21 data (trials 65-70, n=6) shows substantial change requiring immediate analysis. Quick calculation: day 21 mean ≈ 2.6940, notably lower than recent days and very close to baseline 2.6978. This represents a strong relaxation toward baseline after the oscillating elevated pattern of days 13-19. The new overall post-baseline statistics (n=36, z=1.80) show reduced significance compared to my previous z=2.20 calculation, indicating the anomaly is weakening. This temporal evolution—initial elevation, partial relaxation day 16, renewed elevation day 17-19, now strong relaxation day 21—provides critical new evidence for discriminating between environmental cycling (which predicts such reversible oscillations) versus sustained mechanisms like mechanical degradation (which predict monotonic or sustained shifts). Need to update probabilities before collecting more data, as the pattern may be resolving naturally and my hypothesis weights should reflect this changing evidence structure.

Day 23 measurement continues the temporal monitoring program essential for distinguishing between environmental cycling (p=0.58) and sustained shift hypotheses. Day 21 showed relaxation to mean 2.6940, closer to baseline 2.6978 than the day 17/19 elevation (~2.7145). If environmental cycling hypothesis is correct, I expect continued oscillation—either sustained relaxation toward baseline or renewed elevation beginning. Six trials provides adequate statistical power for daily mean while maintaining efficiency. This is standard calibration maintenance, not exotic investigation—tracking instrument behavior is core laboratory practice regardless of cause.

Day 23 data (trials 71-76, n=6) shows mean 2.6897, which represents significant relaxation from the day 17/19 elevation (~2.7145) and is now BELOW the baseline mean of 2.6978. This is a critical development: the resonator has cycled from elevation to below-baseline for the first time in the post-baseline period. The overall z-score has also dropped from 1.80 to 1.38, indicating the anomaly is weakening. The oscillation pattern now spans: baseline (2.6978) → day 16 near-baseline (2.6854) → day 17/19 elevation (2.7145) → day 21 partial relaxation (2.6940) → day 23 below-baseline (2.6897). This below-baseline excursion strongly supports the environmental cycling hypothesis and essentially rules out sustained temperature increase. I need to recalculate statistics with the new data and update probability distributions before taking further action.

Day 25 measurement critical for testing environmental cycling hypothesis. Pattern predicts: day 16 baseline (2.6922), day 17/19 elevation (~2.7145), day 21 relaxation (2.6940), day 23 continued relaxation (2.6897). If cycling hypothesis correct, expect either continued relaxation toward/below baseline or initiation of new elevation phase, establishing ~7-9 day periodicity. This measurement will either confirm the multi-day oscillation pattern (strengthening p=0.64 environmental cycling) or show deviation that requires hypothesis revision. Standard 6-trial session maintains measurement consistency and provides sufficient statistical power to detect position within cycle.

Day 26 measurement critical for testing environmental cycling hypothesis. Day 25 data (events 77-82, mean 2.6879) showed continued relaxation toward baseline after day 17/19 peaks, consistent with predicted ~3-5 day oscillation period. If cycling hypothesis is correct, measurements should either continue relaxing toward/below baseline or begin upturn for next cycle. This timing is crucial: day 26 is ~9 days post-peak (day 17) and ~5 days post-relaxation start (day 21), making it the expected inflection point. Six trials provide adequate statistical power to detect direction of trend while maintaining instrument availability for other settlement duties.

Days 25-26 data (events 80-88) require immediate analysis. Day 25 mean appears ~2.69, day 26 mean also ~2.69 with range 2.6652-2.7229. This represents continued relaxation from day 23 (mean 2.6897), now extending the downward trend over 3 measurement sessions (days 21→23→25/26). The overall z-score has dropped dramatically from previous z=2.20 to current z=0.71, indicating the resonator mean is now approaching baseline closely. This pattern—initial elevation days 13-19 followed by sustained relaxation days 21-26—may be completing a single oscillation cycle rather than the rapid 3-5 day cycling I had inferred. Need to recalculate statistics with full dataset, reassess whether this represents end of transient perturbation vs. longer-period oscillation, and update probability distribution accordingly. The convergence toward baseline is the most significant development since day 13 and fundamentally changes the temporal interpretation.

Day 28 measurement is critical for testing environmental cycling hypothesis. Days 25-26 showed mean 2.6915, approaching baseline (2.6978) after completing relaxation from day 17/19 peak (~2.7145). If the ~9-day cycle continues, I expect day 28 to remain near or slightly below baseline, potentially beginning next elevation phase. Six trials provides adequate statistical power while maintaining instrument longevity. This measurement will either: (1) confirm completion of full cycle with return to baseline, strongly supporting p=0.70 environmental cycling hypothesis, or (2) show unexpected deviation requiring hypothesis revision. The multi-day pattern is now sufficiently well-characterized that today's data will be highly diagnostic.

Day 28 data (events 89-94, n=6) requires immediate analysis. Quick calculation shows mean ≈2.6960, which represents a significant reversal from the days 25-26 relaxation trend (mean 2.6915). If the environmental cycling hypothesis (p=0.70) is correct and we completed one cycle returning to baseline, I would expect continued stability near baseline or the start of a new elevation phase. Instead, day 28 shows renewed elevation above days 25-26 but still below the day 17/19 peak. This could indicate: (a) start of second cycle with shorter period than first, (b) irregular cycling pattern, or (c) shift away from simple periodic hypothesis. The within-day variance also appears high (range 2.6709-2.7168, span of 0.0459) compared to typical measurement scatter. Need to update my z-score for overall post-baseline drift, recalculate the temporal pattern statistics, and reassess whether the cycling hypothesis still best explains the full dataset or whether I need to consider non-periodic environmental effects or return probability mass to mounting stress hypothesis. This is critical before collecting more data.

Day 30 measurement critical for testing periodic hypothesis. If environmental cycling with ~7-9 day period is correct, should observe continued elevation similar to day 28 (mean 2.7010) as we are still in the elevated phase of the second cycle. A return to baseline values would contradict the periodic pattern and require substantial hypothesis revision. Six trials maintains consistency with recent measurement sessions and provides sufficient statistical power to detect deviation from both baseline (2.6978) and day 28 elevated mean. This measurement completes the observational coverage needed to characterize the second cycle peak.

state.question: Why do both pendulum and resonator measurements show substantially increased variance during days 6-10 compared to days 1-5?

hypotheses.label: Environmental conditions changed around day 6 (temperature, humidity, or pressure fluctuations affecting both labs)
hypotheses.rationale: Both instruments show increased scatter starting day 6. Pendulum period depends on thermal expansion of the rod and air density; resonator frequency depends on temperature and humidity. A common environmental cause would affect both. Days 1-5 trials (not individually listed but contributing to baseline) must have been tighter to yield the reported means. The timing coincidence across independent instruments is notable.

hypotheses.label: Measurement technique degraded or changed (observer fatigue, timing method drift, different observers)
hypotheses.rationale: Ten days of continuous trials could lead to protocol drift, fatigue in manual timing, or handoff to less experienced personnel. Would affect both labs if procedures or personnel are shared. However, I maintain detailed protocols specifically to prevent this, making it less likely than environmental causes but not negligible.

hypotheses.label: Instrumentation developed mechanical issues (pendulum pivot wear, resonator mounting looseness)
hypotheses.rationale: Increased variance could indicate degrading knife-edge bearings on the pendulum or mounting instability in the resonator. However, this would require coincidental simultaneous degradation in both independent apparatuses, which strains credibility. More likely to see drift in mean rather than just increased variance.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Replaced 'no active hypotheses' with analysis of variance anomaly. Days 6-10 show visibly larger scatter in both labs compared to what the baseline means imply for days 1-5. The coincident timing across independent instruments points toward environmental causes (45%), though procedural drift (30%) and mechanical degradation (15%) remain plausible. Need to: (1) review days 1-5 individual trial data to confirm variance increase, (2) check environmental logs for HVAC changes or weather events around day 6, (3) verify measurement protocols haven't drifted, (4) inspect both instruments for mechanical wear.

state.question: Why has the resonator_lab measurement shifted significantly upward (z=3.35) in post-baseline trials while pendulum_lab shows no significant shift (z=0.87)?

hypotheses.label: Temperature increase in resonator_lab environment specifically
hypotheses.rationale: The resonator shows a strong systematic upward shift (mean 2.6978→2.7322, z=3.35) while pendulum shows only noise-level drift (mean 1.6646→1.6699, z=0.87). Resonator frequency is highly temperature-sensitive. If resonator_lab experienced a local temperature increase around day 11-13 while pendulum_lab did not, this would explain the divergent behavior. All six post-baseline resonator trials (events 207-212) are elevated above baseline mean, with values ranging 2.7121-2.7637 vs baseline 2.6978. This is a systematic shift, not increased variance.

hypotheses.label: Resonator mounting or apparatus degradation
hypotheses.rationale: Mechanical loosening, mounting stress, or material fatigue in the resonator could produce systematic frequency increase. The shift appears post-day-10, suggesting a discrete change rather than gradual drift. However, well-maintained precision equipment rarely shows abrupt calibration shifts without obvious physical cause. Would require inspection to confirm.

hypotheses.label: Measurement protocol change in resonator_lab only
hypotheses.rationale: If counting method, trigger threshold, or timing protocol changed specifically for resonator measurements after day 10, this could produce systematic shift. However, I maintain strict protocols and would have documented any intentional changes. Unintentional drift is possible but would be unprofessional given my standards.

hypotheses.label: Physical change to local gravitational or electromagnetic environment affecting resonator differentially
hypotheses.rationale: Exotic explanation inconsistent with my epistemic priors. Would require resonator to be sensitive to fields that pendulum is not, which seems implausible for mechanical oscillators. Mentioning only for completeness given settlement's frontier context, but evidence threshold for accepting this is extremely high.
